Q: What is a denial-of-service (DoS) attack?
Option2: An attempt to make a service unavailable by overwhelming resources or exploiting faults

Q: What is a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack?
Option1: A DoS from one tester only
Option2: A DoS launched from many compromised systems (botnets) simultaneously

Q: What is virtual local area network (VLAN) hopping?
Option1: Moving a device between wall jacks
Option2: An attack that forces traffic to move between virtual local area networks by abusing trunking or misconfigurations

Q: What is Media Access Control (MAC) flooding?
Option2: Overloading a switch’s content-addressable memory with many fake addresses so it fails open and floods frames

Q: What is Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) poisoning?
Option2: Inserting false Address Resolution Protocol mappings so traffic is misdirected through an attacker

Q: What is Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) spoofing?
Option1: Deleting the Address Resolution Protocol cache
Option2: Impersonating another host’s Address Resolution Protocol identity to receive traffic intended for that host

Q: What distinguishes ARP poisoning from ARP spoofing?
Option2: Poisoning corrupts mappings in victims’ caches; spoofing claims another’s identity to attract traffic—often used together

Q: What is Domain Name System poisoning?
Option2: Corrupting name-to-address data so clients are directed to malicious destinations

Q: What is Domain Name System spoofing?
Option2: Forging Domain Name System responses to provide false answers to queries

Q: What are rogue devices/services in this context?
Option1: Devices installed by the network team
Option2: Unauthorized equipment or services (for example, a rogue Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol server or rogue access point) that impersonate or bypass controls

Q: What is a rogue Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) server attack?
Option2: An unauthorized server handing out addresses/gateways to divert or disrupt traffic

Q: What is a rogue access point (AP)?
Option2: An unauthorized wireless access point that bypasses network security or imitates the legitimate network

Q: What is an evil twin?
Option2: A malicious access point mimicking a legitimate service set identifier to lure clients

Q: What is an on-path attack?
Option2: Intercepting/altering traffic between two parties while appearing transparent to them
Option3: Blocking all traffic with an access control list

Q: What is phishing?
Option2: Deceiving users into revealing information or performing actions via fraudulent messages

Q: What is dumpster diving?
Option2: Searching discarded materials for sensitive information
Option4: A way to cool data centers

Q: What is shoulder surfing?
Option2: Observing someone’s screen or keyboard to capture information

Q: What is tailgating?
Option2: Following an authorized person into a restricted area without proper authentication
Option3: Installing a tail light on a rack

Q: What is malware?
Option2: Malicious software such as viruses, worms, trojans, or ransomware intended to damage, disrupt, or steal

Q: Which control best reduces impact of a rogue Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol server?
Option2: Enable Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol snooping on switches to trust only authorized ports

Q: Which measure most directly mitigates VLAN hopping?
Option1: Use the same native VLAN everywhere
Option2: Disable unused ports and avoid using the default native VLAN on trunks; explicitly configure trunks and access ports

Q: Which control best counters MAC flooding?
Option2: Port security limits (for example, maximum Media Access Control addresses) and violation actions on switch ports
Option4: Use Domain Name System over HTTPS

Q: Which approach reduces exposure to on-path attacks on web traffic?
Option2: Transport Layer Security with certificate validation and strong cipher suites

Q: Which control reduces user-focused social-engineering success?
Option2: Security awareness training combined with technical controls such as email filtering and multi-factor authentication
